title: A natural OutputP versus IncP separation from clique-free domination
formal:
Does \(\mathrm{TFNP}\ne\mathrm{FP}\) imply that there is a fixed integer \(t\ge3\) for which enumerating all inclusion-minimal dominating sets of \(K_t\)-free graphs belongs to \(\mathrm{OutputP}\) but not to \(\mathrm{IncP}\)?

The graph is explicitly given. Enumeration is deterministic, without repetitions and in any order. Total output-polynomial time is already known for every fixed \(t\); the question is whether this specific family supplies the conditional failure of incremental polynomial time.
why: This would locate the gap between efficient total enumeration and efficient initial output in a standard graph problem. The concrete candidate tests whether a known abstract total-search separation can be realized without constructing artificial padded solution sets.
status_note: The source leaves the natural-example request open and explicitly proposes this graph candidate. The card now selects that candidate with the stated TFNP ≠ FP hypothesis, an announced editorial default after an unanswered optional question. Output-polynomial enumeration is known for every fixed t, but the checked later subclass result does not settle incremental enumeration for all K_t-free graphs. The exact conditional implication is an editorial specialization, not a theorem claimed by the source.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-17; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Capelli and Strozecki prove that OutputP = IncP is equivalent to polynomial-time solvability of all TFNP search relations; their separation construction uses padding.
Bonamy and coauthors give output-polynomial, polynomial-space enumeration of minimal dominating sets for every fixed forbidden clique size, within a larger graph-class theorem.
The habilitation, deposited on arXiv in 2023, poses the natural-example request and mentions the clique-free domination problem as a candidate rather than an established separation.
The WADS paper improves the chordal-bipartite subclass to polynomial delay and space, while its introduction retains the bounded-clique-number output-polynomial benchmark.

sentences: For a fixed forbidden clique size, the task is to list every inclusion-minimal dominating set of the input graph once.
An algorithm with total running time polynomial in the input and the entire output is already known.
The question asks whether TFNP ≠ FP forces some fixed clique size for which no algorithm produces every initial output segment in incremental polynomial time.
This selects the concrete graph candidate suggested by the source instead of imposing an undefined condition of naturalness.
The existing abstract separation and algorithms for smaller graph classes do not settle this implication, whose proof or refutation must be Lean-checked.

definitions:
An enumeration problem is a binary relation \(A(x,y)\) on finite bit strings, with the finite solution set \(A(x)=\{y:A(x,y)\}\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{EnumP}\) when membership in the relation is decidable in deterministic polynomial time and a fixed polynomial \(p\) bounds every solution length by \(p(|x|)\). A correct enumeration algorithm lists each solution once, lists nothing else, and terminates. No output ordering is required.

Enumeration algorithms are uniform deterministic random-access machines with a fixed finite program and integer registers, direct and indirect addressing, branching, comparison, addition, subtraction and multiplication. Each arithmetic or comparison instruction on integers \(a,b\) costs \(1+\lceil\log_2(|a|+|b|+1)\rceil\); other basic instructions cost one. This is the source's bit-sensitive arithmetic convention, with unit-cost random access. Register contents initially vanish, except for an explicit finite encoding of the input. Output writes a finite binary string to an external stream, which cannot be read back as free storage. Charge for writing its bits as well; solution lengths are polynomial in input length. There is no randomization, oracle, advice or imposed working-space bound. We include initial and terminal work. An empty solution set must be recognized within polynomial input time.

Put \(n=|x|\) and \(N=|A(x)|\). The class \(\mathrm{OutputP}\) consists of problems in EnumP admitting a correct algorithm whose total time, including termination, is at most \(C(n+N+1)^d\), with fixed positive constants \(C,d\). The class \(\mathrm{IncP}\) requires an algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that the time from the beginning through the first \(k\) outputs is at most \(C(n+1)^b(k+1)^a\), for every input and every \(1\leq k\leq N\), with a polynomial bound in \(n+N\) for termination. Polynomial preprocessing is included. Constants depend on the relation, never on \(x,k\). The number of outputs and their total encoded length give equivalent polynomial measures because the solutions are distinct and polynomially bounded in length. These definitions give \(\mathrm{IncP}\subseteq\mathrm{OutputP}\).

The search problem \(\mathrm{AnotherSol}_A\) takes \(x\) and an explicitly listed finite set \(S\) of strings, and returns a member of \(A(x)\setminus S\) or a distinguished symbol certifying this difference is empty. Input size counts all bits of the list. Its decision version only asks whether this difference is nonempty. The class TFNP consists of polynomial-time decidable, polynomially balanced relations \(R(x,y)\) with at least one valid \(y\) for every \(x\). Writing TFNP = FP means that every such relation has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm selecting one valid witness; it does not mean counting or listing all valid witnesses.

For the proposed graph candidate, \(G\) is a finite simple undirected graph on \([n]\), explicitly encoded by its adjacency matrix and vertex count. A set \(D\subseteq[n]\) is dominating if every vertex belongs to \(D\) or has a neighbour in \(D\). It is inclusion-minimal if no proper subset is dominating; it need not have minimum cardinality among all dominating sets. A \(K_t\)-free graph has no set of \(t\) pairwise adjacent vertices. For each fixed positive integer \(t\), the associated enumeration problem lists all its inclusion-minimal dominating sets as distinct \(n\)-bit characteristic vectors. Invalid graphs or graphs violating the restriction can be assigned empty output, since validity is polynomial-time testable for fixed \(t\). In the known output-polynomial theorem, \(t\) is fixed before inputs and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Although the source algorithm does not require knowing \(t\), its theorem does not assert a common polynomial bound for arbitrary variable \(t\).

Write \(\mathrm{Dom}_t\) for the enumeration relation for \(K_t\)-free graphs just defined, with \(t\ge3\) fixed. The selected assertion is
\[
\mathrm{TFNP}\ne\mathrm{FP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists t\ge3:\ \mathrm{Dom}_t\in\mathrm{OutputP}\setminus\mathrm{IncP}.
\]
Here \(\mathrm{TFNP}\ne\mathrm{FP}\) means that at least one polynomially balanced, polynomial-time checkable total search relation has no deterministic polynomial-time witness selector. No completeness assumption about TFNP is made. The existential quantifier chooses one fixed integer \(t\), not an input-dependent clique bound. Failure of IncP excludes every uniform deterministic enumerator and every fixed pair of polynomial exponents in the definition. No extra informal test of naturalness or required search-reduction notion is part of this selected target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated implication. An affirmative answer must establish the conditional existence of a fixed t, retain the output-polynomial upper bound and rule out every incremental-polynomial enumerator for that relation. A negative answer must establish TFNP ≠ FP together with incremental-polynomial enumerability for every fixed t ≥ 3. The existing padded construction for an arbitrary enumeration relation does not settle this candidate-specific implication, and neither does slow behavior of a particular domination algorithm.

source_formulation.text: Open problem 3.1 requests a natural OutputP problem outside IncP and suggests minimal dominating sets in graphs excluding a fixed clique. This card adopts that candidate and asks for the separation under TFNP ≠ FP.

context_blocks.text: Output-polynomial total time permits a long initial wait when the eventual output is very large. Incremental polynomial time instead limits the cost of producing each initial segment in terms of the input and that segment’s length. The source asks for a naturally occurring problem witnessing this difference, beyond constructions tailored to separate classes.

Capelli and Strozecki prove that OutputP equals IncP exactly when every TFNP search problem has a polynomial-time solution selector. Hence a bare separation is not an unconditional consequence of that theorem: it is equivalent to a major unresolved total-search separation. The shorthand claim of strict containment in the paragraph before Open problem 3.1 must be read with this hypothesis, not as a proved unconditional strictness.

The proof constructs an output-polynomial enumeration problem from any total search relation by attaching many padding strings to every witness. Exhaustive generation becomes polynomial in the enlarged total output, while an incremental algorithm would reveal an original witness quickly. This explains the abstract conditional separation but does not satisfy the source’s further request for a natural problem.

For any problem already in OutputP, completeness of an explicit candidate solution list can be tested in polynomial time in the input and that list. Simulate an output-polynomial algorithm for its time bound at the list size: if it has not terminated, there must be more solutions than listed; if it has terminated, compare all its outputs with the list. The challenge can therefore remain finding another witness despite easy existence testing for another witness.

Bonamy and coauthors prove output-polynomial enumeration and polynomial working space for every fixed forbidden clique size; their main theorem covers a larger graph class excluding a clique disjoint from one edge. This supplies the positive half of the proposed example, but an upper bound on total time does not prove absence of an incremental algorithm. Minimality here is by set inclusion, so the problem does not ask for a smallest dominating set.

This card adopts the graph candidate suggested in the source and asks for its conditional separation under TFNP ≠ FP. That is a precise specialization of the source’s broader natural-example request; the known abstract separation does not ensure that this particular candidate witnesses it.

The WADS 2025 paper gives polynomial delay and polynomial space for chordal bipartite graphs. Its introduction still lists the bounded-clique-number result as output-polynomial. An upper bound on that special bipartite subclass does not cover all graphs with a fixed forbidden clique.
